text: Other carriers agree with the premise that there has been a relocation of business in the suburbs but argue that this business activity is not necessarily related to the economic life of the center city. They contend that this relationship must be shown before expansion of commercial zones is justified. Some short-haul carriers argue that since there has been no showing that existing regulated short-haul service is inadequate, the present regulations should not be changed. They assert that zone expansion is tantamount to deregulation of their operations, allowing exempt carriers to compete with them. They express fears that cutthroat competition will cause them serious financial harm and ultimately result in deterioration of service to the public. They argue that brokers will spring up in the exempt zones and tender traffic to the carrier offering the lowest rates, regardless of its compliance with safety regulations or claims settlement procedures. They assert that expansion will also benefit freight forwarders to the detriment of the regulated shorthaul carriers. Carriers which possess authority described in terms of a radius around a point argue that they should be compensated for the lost of authority caused by expansion of the commercial zone by being given new authority or by being allowed to extend the radius of their authority by a distance equal to the expansion of the commercial zone. Irregular route carriers argue that commercial zone expansion is inequitable because it will enlarge the authority of regular-route carriers without giving an equivalent benefit to irregular route carriers.
